questions.question: Define isotopes, isobars and isotones with one example each.
questions.solution: Isotopes: same Z (protons), different A — ¹H and ²H. Isobars: same A (total nucleons), different Z — ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N. Isotones: same N (neutrons), different Z and A — ³H and ⁴He (N = 2 each). The three axes of the nuclear chart: Z, A, N.

questions.question: A helium-4 nucleus weighs less than 2 protons + 2 neutrons. Where did the mass go, and what does the difference measure?
questions.solution: The missing mass became BINDING ENERGY when the nucleons fused: Δm·c² is the energy released on assembly — equivalently the energy needed to pull the nucleus apart. Helium's large binding energy per nucleon (~7 MeV) is why fusion releases energy. Mass defect = binding energy/c².

questions.question: Compare α, β and γ radiation in composition, penetrating power and what each changes in the parent nucleus.
questions.solution: α: helium nucleus (2p+2n), stopped by paper; emission lowers Z by 2 and A by 4. β: electron (or positron) from nucleon conversion, stopped by aluminium; β⁻ raises Z by 1, A unchanged (a neutron becomes a proton). γ: high-energy photon, stopped by lead; changes nothing in Z or A — it carries off excess energy after α/β. Penetrating power rises with decreasing charge/mass.

questions.question: A sample's activity halves every 8 days. After 24 days, what fraction remains active, and why does the decay never truly reach zero?
questions.solution: 24 days = 3 half-lives → (½)³ = 1/8 remains. Exponential decay is asymptotic: each half-life multiplies by ½, never by 0 — a nonzero population always has some decay probability per unit time. In practice 'zero' means below detection, not mathematically zero.

questions.concept: Fusion vs fission — why both release energy
questions.question: How can both splitting heavy nuclei and merging light nuclei release energy? Use the binding energy curve.
questions.solution: Both processes move nuclei TOWARD the peak of the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve (around iron). Heavy nuclei (uranium) sit left of the peak's right side — splitting into mid-mass fragments increases binding per nucleon, releasing energy. Light nuclei (hydrogen) sit below the peak — fusing them increases it. The curve, not the direction of the process, decides.

questions.question: Protons in a nucleus repel each other Coulomb-wise, yet most nuclei are stable. Why does the nucleus not fly apart?
questions.solution: The strong nuclear force is attractive between nucleons, short-ranged (~fm) but far stronger than Coulomb repulsion at those separations. Within a nucleus each nucleon bonds to several neighbours, and the total strong attraction exceeds the total electrostatic repulsion. Stability depends on the balance — the more protons, the more neutrons are needed to add attraction without adding charge.

questions.concept: Why binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron
questions.question: Binding energy per nucleon rises to a maximum around iron-56 then falls for heavier nuclei. Why does this explain BOTH fusion and fission energy release?
questions.solution: Systems move toward the most tightly bound state, which is at iron. Light nuclei fuse upward toward the peak, releasing energy; very heavy nuclei split toward the peak, also releasing energy. The curve's shape is the single reason fusion powers stars and fission powers reactors, and why iron is the endpoint of stellar burning. Energy release is always motion toward higher binding energy per nucleon.

questions.question: A helium nucleus weighs less than two protons plus two neutrons. Where has the missing mass gone?
questions.solution: It was converted to binding energy, released as photons when the nucleus formed: ΔE = Δmc². The nucleus is in a lower energy state than free nucleons, and that energy difference shows up as a mass difference. Mass and energy are two accounts of the same quantity. The mass defect isn't lost — it is the nucleus's binding account.
